lines.say: Each qubit you measure gives a zero or a one. So how many results can ten qubits give?
Picture a combination lock where every wheel has two positions, zero and one.
One wheel gives two settings. A second wheel makes four.
Zero zero, zero one, one zero, and one one.
A third wheel makes eight, and every new wheel doubles the count again.
So ten wheels give two to the power of ten, one thousand and twenty four.
Qubits count the same way. Ten qubits have one thousand and twenty four possible results.
Now the quantum part. The qubits hold a number for each result, called an amplitude.
Each amplitude sets how likely its result is, so ten qubits carry one thousand and twenty four of them.
That doubling is where a quantum computer gets its room to work.
But here the lock picture breaks. A lock is only ever set to one combination.
Qubits carry an amplitude for every combination, yet measuring them shows you just one.
So you can't read out all those amplitudes. You get one string of ten zeros and ones.
One last habit to lock in. Kiss kit, our coding toolkit, numbers its qubits from zero.
When it writes a result, qubit zero goes on the right.
Take two qubits, and flip only qubit zero to one.
Kiss kit shows zero one, not one zero, with qubit zero on the right, like the ones digit in forty two.
So every qubit you add doubles the amplitudes, but a measurement still shows you just one string.
